newsitem.title: USA: Former drug firm head charged with insider trading.
newsitem.headline: Former drug firm head charged with insider trading.

text.p: Federal regulators Wednesday charged the former president of Halsey Drug Co. Inc. with concealing embarrassing information about the company and dumping its stock before making a damaging disclosure.

Jay Marcus, who is currently in prison, sold 70,000 shares of the company's stock in February, 1992, about 13 months before disclosing information that nearly halved the price of Halsey's stock, the Securities and Exchange Commission said.

In a complaint filed in U.S. District Court in Brooklyn, N.Y., the SEC said Marcus knew since at least January 1990 that Halsey made and sold certain adulterated generic drugs -- and that the adulteration was being concealed from federal regulators and the public.
After disclosing on March 30, 1993, that it made and sold adulterated drugs, Halsey's stock fell by about 49 percent, the SEC said.
Daniel Goldstein, assistant regional director of the SEC's New York office, said Marcus knew of the adulteration when he sold his 70,000 shares in February 1992 for $565,000.
Goldstein declined to say how much of a loss Marcus avoided by allegedly dumping the stock before the damaging revelation was made.
"The losses he avoided were substantial," he said.

Marcus and other Halsey executives were indicted by a federal grand jury in Baltimore in July 1993 on criminal charges of shipping adulterated drugs across state lines, making false statements to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and conspiring to obstruct its inspection.
He is currently serving a sentence in Lewisburg federal prison after having pleaded guilty to charges stemming from the indictment, according to his lawyer, Frederick Dettmer.
Dettmer declined to comment on the SEC civil charges, saying he had not yet received the complaint.

The SEC said it is seeking to recoup the money Marcus allegedly avoided losing, additional civil insider trading penalties that could be as great as three times the avoided loss, and up to $100,000 for allegedly filing a false and misleading 1991 annual report.

The agency said it also is asking the court to issue an order permanently enjoining Marcus against future violations of federal securities laws and an order barring him from serving as an officer or director of a public company.

Meanwhile, Halsey, which is based in Brooklyn, and the SEC settled an administrative proceeding in which the agency found that the company filed false and misleading reports for the years 1990 and 1991 that failed to disclose that it was not making drugs according to federal standards.
Halsey neither admitted nor denied the findings, but consented to an order by the SEC that it not commit any future violation of federal antifraud and reporting provisions.
In July 1993, Halsey was sentenced to pay a $2.5 million fine after pleading guilty to five felony counts of adulterating the heart medication Quinidine Gluconate.
